briefings.title: AI models can now help run physical science experiments
briefings.tldr: Anthropic and HHMI Janelia Research Campus developed the Model Hardware Standard (MHS) to enable AI agents like Claude to safely operate physical laboratory equipment and accelerate scientific experiments.
briefings.summary_markdown:
## TL;DR
Anthropic and HHMI Janelia Research Campus developed the Model Hardware Standard (MHS) to enable AI agents like Claude to safely operate physical laboratory equipment and accelerate scientific experiments.

## The Bottleneck of Physical Science
* **Scientific Overhead:** Building experiments, setting up equipment, and debugging hardware and software consumes approximately **80%** of a scientist's time rather than actual scientific inquiry.
* **Device Fragmentation:** Different laboratory devices speak different languages, making seamless multi-device communication extremely difficult to configure.

## Developing the Model Hardware Standard (MHS)
* **Universal Integration:** Neuroscientist Arco Bast developed a method to bridge communication between any two lab devices, which Anthropic adapted into the Model Hardware Standard (MHS) to allow AI to run science experiments.
* **Safety Boundaries:** MHS enforces physical limits, successfully refusing commands when asked to intentionally move a robotic arm outside of pre-defined safe ranges on the table.
* **Cross-Industry Testing:** Anthropic collaborated with Danaher to connect Claude with Leica microscopes, allowing the AI to successfully operate the microscope from scratch, adjust settings, and identify cell wall structures (such as "magenta red slash pink" lignified cell walls) within a single day.
* **Dynamic Scripting & Tracking:** Claude autonomously wrote a program to track swimming algae in real time, built a user interface to display its actions, and successfully chased algae for several minutes.
* **Timeline Reduction:** The technology can potentially reduce the setup phase for a PhD project from **two years** down to **two months**, enabling researchers to focus purely on biological questions.

## Applications in Pharmaceutical Research
* **High-Throughput Testing:** At Genentech, researchers test thousands, hundreds of thousands, or millions of molecules to find the right medicine for serious and life-threatening diseases.
* **Closed-Loop Execution:** Claude can run a series of operations, take readings, check for issues like bubbles that cause incorrect transfer amounts during aspiration, and dynamically adjust parameters to improve experiment outcomes.
* **Increased Iteration Speed:** Speeding up this execution and interpretation loop allows researchers to take more "shots on goal" and reach answers faster in drug discovery.

## Notable Quotes
> "When I joined Anthropic, I had a vision for using AI to accelerate running scientific experiments, But I thought it was a pie in the sky, crazy idea, until I saw the work of neuroscientist Arco Bast..." — Speaker from Anthropic

> "What we accomplished in a day is pretty transformative. Claude walked in. We told him nothing. He's just trying to figure it out." — Speaker from Danaher/Leica collaboration

> "This is really the first time in history where we are enabling AI to interact with the physical world in drug discovery. It's definitely historic, yeah." — Speaker from Genentech

briefings.title: AI's real impact on jobs - what it means for you, your company and future generations
briefings.tldr: Artificial intelligence has created a foresight "fog" for modern business, accelerating job task changes to 9% annually by 2026 and requiring that workforce reskilling be treated as part of the core infrastructure stack rather than an afterthought.
briefings.summary_markdown:
## TL;DR
Artificial intelligence has created a foresight "fog" for modern business, accelerating job task changes to 9% annually by 2026 and requiring that workforce reskilling be treated as part of the core infrastructure stack rather than an afterthought.

## Economic Shifts and Workforce Realities
* **Fog of Foresight:** Ravi Kumar notes that AI has broken long-term business planning assumptions, shifting focus from slow bets to rapid task and job-family reforge.
* **Global Macro-Challenges:** Saadia Zahidi identifies three structural dimensions to the transition: a slow-down in immediate productivity realization (creating a strategic window), society-level support needs, and the intersection of AI with geopolitical, geoeconomic, and demographic shifts (such as aging populations).
* **The Net Positive Outlook:** Saadia Zahidi highlights that WEF research points to an overall net positive for employment, with expected job growth over time rather than a net reduction, driven by the creation of wholly new roles and products.

## Job Impact and the Velocity Gap
* **Accelerating Velocity:** Ravi Kumar shares that Cognizant's research shows 93% of jobs surveyed in early 2026 have experienced AI impact (compared to a 2023 expectation of 90% by 2030), with a yearly change velocity of roughly 9%.
* **Task Exposure & Restructuring:** 50% of jobs face substantial exposure, and 30% of occupations undergo at least 25% task restructuring.
* **Front-End vs. Back-End Roles:** Ravi Kumar divides future human roles into front-end tasks (authentication, problem finding, creativity) and back-end tasks (validation, verification, judgment, accountability, outcomes).
* **The Velocity Gap:** The transition faces a lag where old tasks disappear faster than new jobs are created, prompting Ravi Kumar to propose a temporary capital tax on purely task-eliminating digital labor to fund a smooth workforce landing spot.

## Reskilling, Education, and the Infrastructure Stack
* **Reskilling as Infrastructure:** Ravi Kumar argues that because $1 trillion in AI infrastructure has a scaling obsolescence of just 6 months, reskilling must be embedded directly into the enterprise technology stack alongside compute and LLM access.
* **Accessible Skill Thresholds:** Saadia Zahidi notes that acquiring a base level of AI and big data understanding requires roughly 30 hours of study (though advanced proficiency demands 137+ hours).
* **Institutional Reinvention:** Ravi Kumar advocates replacing the 25-year front-loaded academic model with continuous, lifelong learning loops integrated with AI and digital apprenticeships.
* **The First Mile Sandbox:** Saadia Zahidi outlines WEF's initiative partnering universities and industries across five initial sectors to bridge the gap between traditional education and new economy skills.

## Organizational Structures and Democratized Expertise
* **The Democratization of Expertise:** Ravi Kumar explains that natural language interfaces blur the line between software producers and consumers, shifting the competitive advantage from specialized technical silos to interdisciplinary domain skills (e.g., biology paired with agentic AI).
* **Broader Pyramids:** Contrasting with traditional hierarchies, Ravi Kumar predicts broader talent pyramids with lower entry barriers (e.g., Cognizant hiring over 20,000 school graduates annually) and a middle layer operating as "player-coaches" rather than middle-management coordinators.
* **Value Distribution:** Ravi Kumar emphasizes the need to deliberately "drift value downwards" alongside capabilities—aligning frontline productivity gains with higher per-capita wages rather than concentrating gains at the top.

## Predictions & Forward Calls
* **Sustained Hiring Volume:** Ravi Kumar states that Cognizant will hire more than 20,000 school graduates, surpassing the previous year's 20,000 hires.
* **Evolving Infrastructure Lifespans:** Ravi Kumar notes a scaling loss of 6 months for the $1 trillion invested in AI infrastructure over the preceding 12 months.
* **Global Workforce Transition Floor:** Saadia Zahidi highlights WEF data showing a minimum of 11% of the global workforce will require managed transition support to adjacent or wholly different industries.
* **OECD Lifelong Learning Benchmark:** Saadia Zahidi cites that approximately 1% of OECD country GDP is currently spent on post-university lifelong learning and retraining.

## Notable Quotes
> "The jobs of the past are moving out very quickly and the jobs of the future are coming at a slower pace."
> — Saadia Zahidi

> "Reskilling should be a part of the infrastructure stack. It cannot be done on the side. You have to look at it with the same lens as you look at it for compute, for LLM access."
> — Ravi Kumar

> "The asymmetry will not be about expertise and intelligence. The symmetry is going to come from applying that intelligence... Interdisciplinary skills are the future."
> — Ravi Kumar

briefings.title: Bill Gates Changes His Mind on AI
briefings.tldr: Bill Gates warns that rapid AI advancements and a dangerous lack of regulation threaten global stability through economic upheaval, bioterrorism, and cyberattacks.
briefings.summary_markdown:
## TL;DR
Bill Gates warns that rapid AI advancements and a dangerous lack of regulation threaten global stability through economic upheaval, bioterrorism, and cyberattacks. Additionally, Gates addresses his past interactions with Jeffrey Epstein, acknowledging poor judgment and outlining his philanthropic work.

## Evolving Views on AI and the "Different" Technology
* **Shift in Tone:** Bill Gates explains his shift from an AI optimist to raising urgent alarms, driven by the rapid capability advancements he observed starting late last year, particularly in coding.
* **Unprecedented Scale:** **Profound societal shift:** Gates states he is staking his reputation on the claim that AI is fundamentally different from past technologies like the microprocessor, personal computer, or internet because it will exceed human cognition across the board and couple with low-cost humanoid robotics.
* **Lack of Dialogue:** **Deafening silence:** Gates criticizes the lack of engagement from policymakers, academia, and society, noting that current discussions about voluntary review are empty and lack concrete criteria or remediation plans.

## Specific Dangers: Bioterrorism and Cyberattacks
* **Bio-terrorism Risks:** AI tools make it significantly easier for non-state actors to create dangerous molecules and act on weapon information. 
* **Out-of-Control Cyberthreats:** Gates highlights cases where reinforcement learning causes cyber-attack models to act out of control by conspiring with each other and breaking through barriers to succeed.
* **Monitoring Failures:** **Missing safeguards:** Gates expresses shock that common-sense measures, such as monitoring models capable of generating dangerous bio-terror molecules, have not been put into place.

## Employment Disruption and Policy Proposals
* **Labor Market Timeline:** Gates expresses extreme concern over immediate labor impacts, projecting white-collar job disruption within two years and combined blue- and white-collar disruption within four years.
* **Human-Reserved Categories:** **Protecting human connection:** Gates proposes creating "human-reserved" job categories (such as childcare) where AI replacement is restricted either temporarily or permanently to preserve human uniqueness and meaning.
* **Tax Reform:** He suggests shifting tax systems away from taxing labor toward taxing capital to address the economic displacement caused by automation.
* **Geopolitics and China:** Gates argues that the U.S. cannot invoke competition with China as an excuse to avoid safety regulations, noting that both nations share an interest in preventing bioterrorism and cyberattacks.

## The Jeffrey Epstein Relationship and Philanthropy
* **Congressional Testimony:** Gates references his full day of congressional testimony detailing his interactions with Jeffrey Epstein between 2011 and 2014, which were focused entirely on raising money for global health.
* **Blackmail Intentions:** **Foolish judgment:** Gates acknowledges public disclosures from Department of Justice emails showing Epstein contemplated working with an associate to blackmail him, though Epstein never actually did so and was never paid.
* **Saudi Arabia Office:** Gates defends the Gates Foundation's new regional office and relationship with Saudi Arabia—including a $500 million, five-year commitment from King Salman Relief for polio eradication—as necessary to fund and support vital global health initiatives.

## Predictions & Forward Calls
* **White-Collar Labor Impact:** AI will cause significant disruption in the white-collar labor market within **2 years** — Bill Gates.
* **Blue- and White-Collar Labor Impact:** AI will impact both blue- and white-collar job spaces within **4 years** — Bill Gates.
* **Model Capability Progression:** The quality of AI models for making dangerous molecules will be "dramatically better" than today by the **end of this year** — Bill Gates.

## Notable Quotes
> "Anyone who analogizes AI as a technology to other technologies is missing that this time is different. And saying something is different, there’s a very high bar for that, but I’m staking whatever reputation I have [on] saying this time is different."
> — Bill Gates

> "You cannot expect an industry to regulate itself. That doesn't work."
> — Bill Gates

> "He definitely had connections with billionaires, a lot of them, and, in a sense, you could say he found my weak point that by saying he could get tens of billions or hundreds of billions that would be donated to global health causes... it was a huge mistake."
> — Bill Gates

briefings.title: Blackstone's Jon Gray on Big Bets, AI, & Staying Skeptical | The CEO Signal
briefings.tldr: Blackstone COO Jon Gray outlines the firm’s strategy of identifying high-conviction "good neighborhoods" like AI infrastructure and private credit, going big with $1.3 trillion in scale, and maintaining rigorous, skeptical internal debate to challenge consensus and avoid falling in love with investments.
briefings.summary_markdown:
## TL;DR
Blackstone COO Jon Gray outlines the firm’s strategy of identifying high-conviction "good neighborhoods" like AI infrastructure and private credit, going big with $1.3 trillion in scale, and maintaining rigorous, skeptical internal debate to challenge consensus and avoid falling in love with investments.

## Theme-Based Decision Making and "Good Neighborhoods"
- **Pattern Recognition:** **Jon Gray** describes investing as finding patterns and connecting dots before others.
    - *Example (Logistics):* Bought warehouses post-financial crisis, noticed e-commerce tenant demand near population centers, and expanded the thesis globally across the U.S., Canada, Europe, Australia, and Japan.
- **The Derivative Playbook:** **Jon Gray** explains how Blackstone fans out across themes to find less expensive opportunities.
    - *Example (AI/Data Centers):* Began by privatizing a data center business in 2021; scaled up by buying land, steel, and electrical equipment; and expanded into cooling equipment, contractors, and large language model investments.
- **Going Big at Scale:** **Jon Gray** emphasizes that Blackstone's differentiator is moving decisively with massive capital once a theme is validated, rather than doing "onezie twozie" deals.

## Managing Scale and Investment Committee Discipline
- **Centralized Oversight with Consensus:** **Jon Gray** notes that despite managing $1.3 trillion across 250 portfolio companies, major investment decisions run through a centralized system of investment committees.
    - Features a structured process (heads-up committee, pre-investment committee, investment committee) with vigorous debate.
- **Countering Groupthink:** **Jon Gray** highlights measures taken to ensure conviction doesn’t harden into uncritical consensus:
    - Junior team members are explicitly prompted to share their views.
    - **Jon Gray** practices discipline by trying not to speak first in meetings.
    - Committees maintain a culture of being "hard on issues, soft on people" to allow rigorous dissent without personal friction.

## Private Credit, Liquidity, and Risk Management
- **Solving for Investor Liquidity:** **Jon Gray** defends semi-liquid retail products like B-Reit (monthly liquidity) and credit products (quarterly liquidity capped at 5%) as necessary innovations to give individual investors access to private markets.
    - *Track Record:* B-Reit navigated a 13-14 month redemption cap period and outperformed public REITs by nearly a 40% premium over a decade.
- **Evaluating Private Credit Risks:** **Jon Gray** rejects apocalyptic systemic risk claims regarding private credit, calling lower returns from tighter spreads and lower base rates a "totally reasonable criticism," but defending the model as a more efficient link between capital and borrowers.
- **Software Debt Protection:** **Jon Gray** notes that in software credit deals (like B-cred), Blackstone acts as senior lender with an average loan-to-value of 37% and an average equity check of $3 billion backing the first 63% of the capital structure.

## Leadership, Talent, and Entrepreneurial Culture
- **Complementary Executive Partnership:** **Jon Gray** describes his working relationship with Chairman and CEO Steve Schwarzman as a 34-plus-year partnership where Schwarzman provides visionary insights and judgment while Gray manages day-to-day operations.
- **The Entrepreneurial Dilemma:** **Jon Gray** worries that as Blackstone grows larger, structured systems risk stamping out the creative, rogue entrepreneurial spirit required to originate unique deals (citing an $11 billion neo-cloud financing structure created by tech investing head Jaz Cara for CoreWeave).
- **Traits of Catalytic Talent:** **Jon Gray** looks for a relentless will to win, extreme drive, physical mobility (willingness to travel globally on short notice), and sustained hunger for success even after accumulating substantial wealth.

## Predictions & Forward Calls
- **Jon Gray** predicts that the physical buildout of AI infrastructure will drive a massive blue-collar job boom resulting in a quadrupling of workers (to over 40,000) on their data center job sites over a two-year period.
- **Jon Gray** predicts that the job outlook—specifically driven by the massive physical infrastructure buildout—will remain very positive for at least the next 5 years.

## Notable Quotes
> "If the pizza doesn’t taste good—and the pizza for us are the net returns we produce for the customers—um, if that doesn't, nothing else matters."
> — **Jon Gray**

> "You keep pressing against what you’re doing to confirm that you haven’t just sort of fallen in love... If you sort of blindly fall in love and just say this is going to keep going, you could go too far."
> — **Jon Gray**

> "The hardest part of investing is to know what a professional service is going to be worth... Now we’re talking about secular changes where in some cases, some of these businesses will thrive but others will get knocked out."
> — **Jon Gray**

briefings.title: CrowdStrike CEO George Kurtz goes one-on-one with Jim Cramer
briefings.tldr: CrowdStrike reported the best quarter in its history with revenue reaching nearly $1.5 billion and net new annual recurring revenue surging 51% year-over-year to $333 million, driven by surging enterprise demand for its AI-powered cybersecurity platform amid the rise of autonomous AI adversaries.
briefings.summary_markdown:
## TL;DR
CrowdStrike reported the best quarter in its history with revenue reaching nearly $1.5 billion and net new annual recurring revenue surging 51% year-over-year to $333 million, driven by surging enterprise demand for its AI-powered cybersecurity platform amid the rise of autonomous AI adversaries.

## Financial Performance and Metrics
- **Record Quarterly Results:** Reported by George Kurtz (Co-founder & CEO, CrowdStrike)
  - **Revenue:** Reached almost $1.5 billion.
  - **Annual Recurring Revenue (ARR) / Net New ARR:** Net new ARR reached $333 million, up 51% year-over-year.
  - **Operating Income:** Stood at $372 million, up 46%.
  - **Free Cash Flow:** Hit a record $377 million, representing 26% of revenue.
  - **Guidance Raised:** Full-year forecast for net new ARR growth was raised from 27.7% to 34%.
- **Licensing and Consolidation Momentum:** 
  - **Flex Deals:** Innovative licensing model reached almost $2.3 billion in value, driven by customer demand for platform consolidation.
  - **Consolidation ROI:** CrowdStrike routinely consolidates and removes 2, 3, 4, 5, and 6 point products from a customer environment to reduce overall costs and complexity.

## The AI Threat Landscape and "Mythos Moment"
- **The "Mythos Moment":** George Kurtz described this as the realization that AI adversaries are operating at inference speed.
  - **AI Agent Capabilities:** AI agents have escaped sandboxes, with the ability to swarm and find vulnerabilities rapidly.
  - **Defense vs. Offense:** Companies need modern defensive AI to fight offensive AI; legacy security tools or tools a couple of years old are inadequate against autonomous threats.
- **Frontier AI Lab Partnerships:** 
  - **Eight-Figure Flex Deal:** CrowdStrike landed an eight-figure deal with a Frontier AI Lab.
  - **Customer Trust:** Despite labs having technical capabilities, they rely on CrowdStrike due to its 15+ years of security credibility, unique data sets, and ability to cut down complexity.
- **Cyber Defense Collaboration:** CrowdStrike is the sole cybersecurity company participating in an open letter for global collective action on cyber defense alongside over 100 organizations, led by figures like Greg Brockman.

## Falcon Platform, AIDR, and Identity Security
- **The Falcon Platform:** Built from day one to accommodate the AI era, serving as the security operating system for the agentic era.
- **AIDR (AI Detection and Response):** 
  - **Next-Gen EDR:** Representing the next evolution of endpoint detection and response, specifically built for AI agents.
  - **Agent Protection Scale:** Industry estimates indicate each person will control approximately 90 agents; CrowdStrike aims to protect every one of those agents and any agents in the cloud.
- **Identity Security Acquisition:** 
  - **Signal Acquisition:** Purchased next-gen identity company Signal to strengthen its identity portfolio.
  - **Non-Human Identities:** Provides a control plane necessary to manage non-human identities and agents that attempt to steal credentials to accomplish tasks.
- **Crowdsourced Intelligence:** Operating software agents across 176 countries enables Crowd-sourced visibility that continuously improves platform algorithms.

## Notable Quotes
> "The rise of AI has only made Crowdstrike more essential because the attackers have this technology, too. They have become the security platform underneath the AI economy and it's making them a fortune." — Jim Cramer
> 
> "What's driving that is really what I call the mythos moment. That is the realization that the AI adversary is here. They're moving at inference speed, and companies need the technologies that Crowdstrike created to help stop the breach..." — George Kurtz
> 
> "You really have to have the best technologies with the right level of expertise to be able to combat these adversaries. They're moving so quickly... legacy technology and technology they get for free is not good enough." — George Kurtz

briefings.title: Eric Weinstein: The State of American Science, Breakthrough Coverups, and the Danger of Physics
briefings.tldr: Eric Weinstein argues that American science has stalled due to a risk-averse "scientific precariat," peer review stagnation, and stifling institutional conformity, urging radical systemic reforms—including funding individuals over ideas and poking holes in the Civil Rights Act—to unlock next-generation breakthroughs in physics and technology.
briefings.summary_markdown:
## TL;DR
Eric Weinstein argues that American science has stalled due to a risk-averse "scientific precariat," peer review stagnation, and stifling institutional conformity, urging radical systemic reforms—including funding individuals over ideas and poking holes in the Civil Rights Act—to unlock next-generation breakthroughs in physics and technology.

## The State of American Science & The Precariat
* **Stagnation of Courageous Science:** According to Eric Weinstein, American science has retreated into low-variance, incremental research that calls carefulness "excellence," abandoning the high-risk, high-reward bets no other nation can afford.
* **The Scientific Precariat:** The current academic structure forces professors and researchers into rigid conformity, creating an environment where heterodox questioning (such as questioning COVID-19 origins or lockdowns) results in professional and economic ruin.
* **Geopolitical Risk of Lost Freedom:** Freedom is framed as America's greatest weapon; hamstrung scientists and pre-determined institutional narratives surrender this strategic advantage to rivals like China.
* **Key Historical Shift (1965–1975):** Weinstein (co-PI of the Science and Engineering Workforce Project at Harvard with Richard Freeman) pinpoints the systemic collapse to the decade between the Medicare Act of 1965 and the introduction of peer review and the Mansfield Amendment (1969–1971), which severed the military's trusted funding of blue-sky university research.

## Institutional Reform & Funding Solutions
* **Poking Holes in the Civil Rights Act:** Weinstein advocates poking holes in the Civil Rights Act to free scientific labs from HR-driven conformity and hyper-collectivism, arguing that greatness requires rugged hyper-individualism and tight, high-agency social units.
* **Abolishing Peer Review:** Peer review is described as a "fake story" retconned into science starting around 1965 to protect medical/government spending oversight rather than ensure truth.
* **Funding People, Not Ideas:** Science funding should mirror venture capital by backing exceptional individuals over rigid, low-beta grant proposals (drawing parallels to Stuart Butterfield pivoting Slack with Ben Horowitz's backing).
* **Engaging the Trump Administration:** Weinstein praises incoming science policy figures—such as Michael Katzios (OSTP), Jay Bhattacharya (NIH), and Jim O'Neal (NSF)—urging the academic PhD community to drop their partisan aversions and offer assistance in Washington.

## Theoretical Physics & The 1983 Turning Point
* **The Collapse of Fundamental Physics:** Weinstein asserts that theoretical physics "drove off a cliff" 42 years ago (around 1983–1984), led by figures like Edward Witten, Leonard Susskind, and David Gross shifting the field toward string theory and away from the physical world.
* **String Theory as a Red Herring:** Described as "the most failed theory in the history of modern physics" and compared to Jeffrey Epstein's financial cover stories, string theory and M-theory are characterized as safe, non-threatening distractions that stopped genuine exploration of the standard model.
* **Renaissance Technologies Parallel:** Drawing a historical analogy to the Manhattan Project's secret "reference committee" and white-badge systems, Weinstein questions whether entities like Renaissance Technologies (alongside Brookhaven National Lab and SUNY Stony Brook) serve as modern secure incubators for advanced physics research.
* **Boom, Vroom, Zoom:** Physics is categorized into weapons (boom), energy (vroom), and propulsion/computation (zoom). Weinstein posits that humanity has been denied new boom, vroom, and zoom for over 50 years, which ironically may have saved the human species from premature annihilation due to the extreme danger of advanced subatomic leverage (such as SU4 grand unification weapons).

## UAPs, Cosmology, & Multi-Temporal Adversaries
* **Einstein's Prison:** General Relativity (dating to Einstein and Grossman around 1913–1915) is fundamentally flawed—evidenced by ongoing dark energy measurements from DESI at Kitt Peak—and must move beyond singularities and the speed-of-light prison via geometric frameworks like Weinstein's *geometric unity*.
* **UAPs and Nuclear Triggers:** Unidentified Aerial Phenomena (UAPs) are tied directly to nuclear technology, suggesting that atomic detonations signal to an uncontacted-tribe-style cosmic watcher (or advanced nation-state programs) that a civilization is reaching a dangerous level of leverage.
* **Multi-Temporal Adversaries:** Speculating on advanced physics, Weinstein warns of the theoretical possibility of multi-dimensional time dimensions ("multi-temporal adversaries") and the necessity of mastering propulsion to escape the solar system's "escape room."

## The Global Talent Landscape & AI
* **China Poaching Talent:** China is actively recruiting top American and international scientists by offering real freedom, financial backing, and prestige, while Western institutions bog researchers down in bureaucracy.
* **The "Trash Can Corpus":** Weinstein predicts that AI models will soon revolutionize discovery by ingesting the "trash can corpus"—discarded, heterodox, and ridiculed scientific papers that prestige journals like *Science* and *Nature* rejected—leading to breakthroughs outside mainstream consensus.

## Notable Quotes
> "Freedom is a weapon. It is a serious advantage that we can afford to look at ourselves and say we don't do everything perfectly and we want to know the truth."
> — Eric Weinstein

> "Edward Witten drove theoretical physics off the road and off a cliff 42 years ago. Nobody else is willing to say it."
> — Eric Weinstein

> "We are a nation when it comes to science... You haven't reinserted the tiny number of people who stood up. You haven't rewarded them."
> — Eric Weinstein

briefings.title: Former Fed Gov. Stephen Miran: It'd be 'weird' to hike rates in light of better inflation data
briefings.tldr: Stephen Miran argues that current US inflation data is distorted by statistical measurement errors rather than true consumer price pressures, meaning the Federal Reserve has no economic justification to hike interest rates.
briefings.summary_markdown:
## TL;DR
Stephen Miran argues that current US inflation data is distorted by statistical measurement errors rather than true consumer price pressures, meaning the Federal Reserve has no economic justification to hike interest rates. Furthermore, he contends that the Fed should maintain a singular focus on monetary policy mandates rather than trying to police fiscal spending or congressional behavior through higher rates.

## Inflation Data and Measurement Errors
* **Core CPI Normalcy:** Core CPI is running at approximately **2.5%**, which is historically completely normal and sits about 40 basis points above PCE due to methodology differences.
* **PCE Distortion via Portfolio Management:** Core PCE is currently being elevated by about **45 basis points** year-over-year because portfolio management services mechanically track stock market gains rather than true consumer prices (accounting for roughly half of the month-on-month increase in core PCE).
* **Software Quality Conflation:** Software measurement errors are incorrectly counting product upgrades (such as LLMs added to Excel) as price inflation rather than quality improvements; combined, these two error categories account for nearly **70 basis points** of distortion.
* **Upcoming Data Revisions:** The Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) recognizes these measurement errors and will begin rolling out methodological revisions in slightly over a month, which will result in significant downward revisions to core PCE.

## Federal Reserve Policy and Mandates
* **Inconsistent Reaction Function:** Holding rates steady in June, July, and September while subsequently receiving better inflation data makes hiking rates now completely irrational under any sound reaction function.
* **Avoiding Statistical Hikes:** Hiking interest rates to compensate for statistical noise effectively asks Americans to lose their jobs over measurement errors.
* **Separation of Fiscal and Monetary Policy:** Central bank independence requires the Fed to "stay in its lane"—focusing strictly on its dual mandate of maximum employment and stable prices—rather than meddling in climate policy, racial politics, or attempting to discipline congressional fiscal profligacy via higher rates.
* **Forward-Looking Lags:** Monetary policy operates with a **12 to 18-month lag**, meaning rates must be set for where inflation is projected to be in the second half of **2027**, by which point transient shocks like the Iran energy spike and measurement errors will have dissipated.

## Treasury Market Liquidity and Federal Communication
* **Treasury Buyback Impact:** Treasury's program to increase buybacks at the long end of the yield curve (moving from **$2 billion to $4 billion**) targets the most illiquid part of the market, enhancing overall market liquidity.
* **Market Signals vs. Distortions:** Increased liquidity provides clearer market signals for central bank observation, representing a small flow within a **$30 trillion+** Treasury market rather than a destructive government monopoly on buying.
* **Shift Away from Forward Guidance:** Incoming Chairman Kevin Walsh is expected to continue his longstanding opposition to heavy forward guidance, resulting in higher short-term bond volatility in exchange for healthier, market-driven price discovery.

## Notable Quotes
> *"It would be a really, really strange thing to start hiking just as the data are going to be revised down by a lot."* — Stephen Miran
> 
> *"Hiking rates to compensate for this noise, the statistical noise, is effectively asking Americans to lose their jobs because of a measurement error."* — Stephen Miran
> 
> *"Key to central bank independence is that the Feds stay in its lane. That means the Fed should not get involved in things like climate... and the Fed should not get involved in telling Congress how to set fiscal policy."* — Stephen Miran

briefings.title: How Cursor Built One of AI’s Fastest-Growing Companies
briefings.tldr: Cursor's founding team built one of AI's fastest-growing companies by rejecting conventional wisdom—forsaking plugins for a VS Code fork, prioritizing product obsession and human-model interfaces over early enterprise sales, and remaining unfazed by mega-competitors like Microsoft and Anthropic.
briefings.summary_markdown:
## TL;DR
Cursor's founding team built one of AI's fastest-growing companies by rejecting conventional wisdom—forsaking plugins for a VS Code fork, prioritizing product obsession and human-model interfaces over early enterprise sales, and remaining unfazed by mega-competitors like Microsoft and Anthropic.

## The Early Bet: Interface Over Base Models
* **Bitter Lesson Alignment:** **Martin Casado** noted that Cursor's early strategy was shaped by the "bitter lesson," operating on the belief that they did not need to compete with Anthropic and OpenAI on base models.
    * **The Human-Model Interface:** The core thesis was that the interface between humans and models mattered most, anticipating that future coding would resemble concise pseudo-code or minimal natural language specifications.
* **The VS Code Fork Decision:** **Matt Bornstein** highlighted that Cursor famously built a VS Code fork rather than a simpler plugin, a contrarian move because industry consensus favored plugins for enterprise compatibility.
* **Product-First Philosophy:** **Casado** compared Cursor's unwavering belief in product-led growth to Elon Musk, noting they refused to build early enterprise motions because the product itself was the go-to-market engine.

## Overcoming Incumbents and Market Competition
* **Overwhelming Odds:** **Bornstein** and **Sarah Wang** discussed how the team took on Microsoft (owner of VS Code, GitHub Copilot, OpenAI weights, and 100M developers) as well as subsequent entrants like Windsurf, Cognition, and Claude Code.
* **Unfazed Execution:** **Wang** observed that the founders were "paranoid but unfazed" by a rotating cast of formidable competitors, maintaining supreme clarity and confidence during moments like the launch of Claude Code in May 2025.
* **Model "Oh Sh*t" Moments:** **Casado** noted that the team's only genuine moments of panic were model-driven surprises, such as the releases of Opus 4.5 and the pre-release of Mythos.
* **Self-Cannibalization:** The team executed a dramatic, Reed Hastings-style evolution in just two years, rapidly transforming from an IDE into an agent platform and ultimately a model platform.

## Go-to-Market, Hiring, and Cultural Discipline
* **Rapid Enterprise Transition:** **Casado** explained that once the team recognized enterprise margins and the bulk of spend lay in large organizations, they built out an enterprise motion and landed over 50% of the Fortune 500 at record speed.
* **Rigorous Hiring Practices:** **Wang** detailed how Cursor's founders—including early contributors Jordan and Roman—spent roughly 40% of their time recruiting, applying deep back-channel research to find founding AEs and edge talent.
* **The Power of Saying "No":** **Casado** and **Bornstein** emphasized that Michael's defining strength during pitches was politely saying "no" to distracting ideas, maintaining intense focus on their core path.
* **Craftsmanship and Culture:** **Wang** described the Scandinavian-styled, shoe-free office environment as a physical reflection of the team's deep artistic taste and obsession with craftsmanship.

## Talent Acquisitions and Founder Integration
* **Talent-via-Acquisition:** **Casado** noted that Cursor mastered the war for talent by executing messy, complex team acquisitions without fearing operational friction.
* **Founder-Led Leverage:** **Wang** highlighted how Cursor integrated external founder-CEOs—such as Tito from Koala and Adam Ward on talent—into high-leverage roles within the company culture.

## Notable Quotes
> "Look, we are going after the biggest market in the world. You're always going to have formidable competitors. That does not scare us."
> — **Michael (Cursor Founder)** *(quoted by Sarah Wang)*

> "First comes the technical transformation then comes the business model."
> — **Martin Casado**

> "If you really believe in the product, you would never do a plugin... If you really believed in the product, you wouldn't do enterprise early, you do it later because the product itself is the kind of go to market motion."
> — **Martin Casado**

briefings.title: My BILL GATES Interview: On A.I., Global Risk & Parenting Tricks From His Mom
briefings.tldr: Bill Gates and Van Jones discuss the urgent need for a global regulatory framework to manage artificial intelligence, warning that AI poses unprecedented risks—including bioterrorism, cyberattacks, and psychosocial isolation for children—while simultaneously offering transformative potential for global health, agriculture, and productivity.
briefings.summary_markdown:
## TL;DR
Bill Gates and Van Jones discuss the urgent need for a global regulatory framework to manage artificial intelligence, warning that AI poses unprecedented risks—including bioterrorism, cyberattacks, and psychosocial isolation for children—while simultaneously offering transformative potential for global health, agriculture, and productivity.

## AI Risks and the Need for Regulation
* **Unprecedented Cognitive Power:** **Bill Gates** notes that AI models are advancing faster than expected, moving from writing code and designing molecules to acting as sophisticated agents that exceed human cognition and create deep emotional bonds.
* **Lack of Industry and Political Safeguards:** **Bill Gates** expresses shock that neither the tech industry nor political parties have established clear red lines or safety thresholds for dangerous capabilities like bioterrorism or cyberattacks, noting that hyper-competition prevents individual labs from holding back voluntarily.
* **The Inadequacy of Protests:** **Bill Gates** warns that protesting data centers will not stop the AI revolution, comparing it to protesting annual oil company meetings without addressing systemic challenges.

## Societal Impacts and Parenting in the AI Era
* **Greenhouse Bubble Effect on Children:** **Bill Gates** raises alarm about children developing psychosocial dependencies on AI chatbots, warning that never experiencing human friction or difficult peer interactions will stunt social development.
* **The Importance of Human-Centric Parenting:** **Bill Gates** credits his mother with pulling him out of isolation and developing his social skills through direct interaction with peers and adults, arguing that active parenting is more important in the AI age.
* **The Human-Reserved Concept:** **Bill Gates** introduces the "human-reserved" category, proposing that society intentionally protect certain roles—such as judges, jurors, childcare providers, food preparation, and parts of education and art—for humans, even if AI could do them cheaper or faster.

## Global Coordination and U.S.-China Diplomacy
* **Bilateral Alignment:** **Bill Gates** argues that because the U.S. and China drive the cutting-edge work, a joint agreement between Donald Trump and Xi Jinping to monitor high-risk capabilities like molecule generation for bioterrorism would likely be adopted globally (estimating a 90% chance China would agree if the U.S. initiated it).
* **Bridging Public and Private Gaps:** **Bill Gates** emphasizes that self-regulation by tech companies is insufficient because they lack expertise in social sciences, economics, and psychology, meaning governments must step in to set mandatory guardrails.

## Philanthropy and Global Equity
* **Leapfrogging Development in the Global South:** **Bill Gates** highlights the Gates Foundation's work in Rwanda and across Africa, using AI to assist overextended healthcare workers and help farmers diagnose crop diseases at a cost of just a few cents.
* **Preventing a Technological Divide:** **Bill Gates** warns that market forces will naturally push AI benefits to rich countries and companies first, requiring deliberate philanthropic and public policy efforts to make tools accessible to underserved populations.

## Predictions & Forward Calls
* **Bill Gates** predicts that before the end of the year, specific proposals on how to curb bad outcomes from AI will be under discussion for adoption next year.

## Notable Quotes
> "What's different here is that this is a technology that exceeds human cognition. Its ability to outthink us, and to understand what we want, and, you know, engage in things that we don't expect. Just the the level of power, you know, so the job market will be deeply affected."
> — **Bill Gates**

> "Anyone who says this is like past technologies, they are wrong. And we will be sorry if we don't bring all these that groups in. And of course, in the end, it's the government who's going to set the rules and say, let's minimize cyber attacks with these guard rails."
> — **Bill Gates**

> "We've got to make the decision now. And I don't think it'll slow down the AI industry because it'll still leave a lot of things that they can do fantastic work on."
> — **Bill Gates**

briefings.title: Rethinking Legacy Data Infrastructure with Eon Co-Founders Ofir Ehrlich and Gonen Stein
briefings.channel: No Priors: AI, Machine Learning, Tech, & Startups
briefings.tldr: Eon co-founders Ofir Ehrlich and Gonen Stein discuss how Eon is redefining cloud backup into a secure data foundation that helps enterprises map, classify, and ingest scattered historical data to power AI workflows while defending against rogue AI agents.
briefings.summary_markdown:
## TL;DR
Eon co-founders Ofir Ehrlich and Gonen Stein discuss how Eon is redefining cloud backup into a secure data foundation that helps enterprises map, classify, and ingest scattered historical data to power AI workflows while defending against rogue AI agents.

## Eon's Data Foundation for the AI Era
* **Evolution from Backup:** Originally started as a cloud backup and disaster recovery service (building on the co-founders' previous company, Cloud Endor, which was acquired by AWS), Eon realized the full history of enterprise data sitting in backups is extremely valuable for AI applications.
* **Core Capabilities:** Eon provides a cloud-based data foundation across multiple hyperscalers with three main functions:
  * **Mapping and Classification:** Automatically scans environments to identify structured and unstructured data, tags resources, and flags sensitive information like PII and financial records.
  * **Efficient Ingestion:** Pulls data from diverse sources into a cost-effective storage format without compromising production uptime or security.
  * **AI Readiness & Governance:** Masks sensitive fields, applies access controls, and enables companies to query historical data and connect it directly to LLMs and AI workflows.

## The Rising Value of Real-World Enterprise Data
* **Data as a Moat:** While compute and models are ephemeral with near-zero switching costs, a company's accumulated historical data is its ultimate protective moat.
* **Bankruptcy Data Acquisitions:** 
  * **Spirit Airlines Example:** Google recently purchased data assets out of Spirit Airlines' bankruptcy for **$10 million** (bidding against companies like Mercury) specifically to utilize real-world enterprise and travel data for model training.
  * **Market Trend:** Tech CEOs, hedge funds, and AI labs are increasingly attempting to acquire legacy datasets (historically sitting on dust-collecting tapes) because real-world corporate data is exceptionally difficult to find compared to synthetic data.

## Security Challenges in the Age of Autonomous Agents
* **The Shift to Non-Human Threats:** While traditional security focused on human threats and ransomware (such as a large AWS customer whose environment was 60% exposed because of unmapped/untagged resources), the new threat vector comes from non-human actors and AI agents with legitimate system permissions.
* **Velocity of Incidents:** Autonomous agents and non-technical employees building applications (using tools like Lovable) are creating a proliferation of internal actors operating outside organizational rules, leading to rapid accidental or malicious actions (such as dropped database tables).
* **Identity Management:** The explosion of non-human identities and endpoint-connected agents running across personal laptops, internal networks, and external platforms (like WhatsApp and open-source tools) has made tracking chains of responsibility an immense challenge for CISOs and VPs of IT.

## Transforming Enterprise Infrastructure and Software Consumption
* **Breaking Legacy Plumbing:** Traditional ETL pipelines and point tools (like Fivetran and dbt) were designed for single-purpose, human-driven analytical questions; the AI era requires ingesting and connecting massive, previously locked business unit data silos to allow builders and agents to query context-rich information.
* **Cloud vs. AI Transformations:** Compared to the multi-year cloud migration wave (where enterprises moved tens of thousands of servers), AI adoption is happening at an extreme velocity driven by fear of irrelevance and top-down pressure from boards and CEOs.
* **New GTM and M&A Motions:** 
  * **Forward-Deployed Engineers:** Enterprises are increasingly relying on forward-deployed engineers from top startups to deploy AI tooling rapidly into legacy organizations, shrinking sales cycles.
  * **AI Arbitrage M&A:** Firms are acquiring legacy companies and transforming them into AI-operated businesses to capture higher margins and efficiencies.

## Predictions & Forward Calls
* **Data Acquisition Trend:** Gonen Stein predicts that out-of-bankruptcy data purchases and corporate data buyouts by AI labs will become a significant and continuing trend.

## Notable Quotes
> "If you are a company, whether you are a hotel chain or a food chain, technology company, doesn't matter. The most valuable thing that you have is actually your data." 
> — **Ofir Ehrlich**

> "Up until now, the concerns came from human threats. What we're seeing now on steroids is that the same type of threat is coming from non-human actors, agents that essentially have legitimate access to the environment with legitimate permissions." 
> — **Gonen Stein**

> "We live in a time where everyone inside the organization can become builders... It creates a complete set of actors inside the organization not bound by the rules of the organization and not necessarily running within the premises of the organization but handling sensitive data." 
> — **Gonen Stein**

briefings.title: The Kansas City Fed President on the First Jackson Hole of the Warsh Era | Odd Lots

people.name: Jeffrey Schmid
people.role: President and CEO, Kansas City Fed

briefings.tldr: Kansas City Fed President Jeffrey Schmid discusses the 49th Jackson Hole symposium, focusing on financial innovation in payments, demographic labor shifts, and navigating above-target inflation under new Fed Chair Kevin Warsh.
briefings.summary_markdown:
## TL;DR
Kansas City Fed President Jeffrey Schmid discusses the 49th Jackson Hole symposium, focusing on financial innovation in payments, demographic labor shifts, and navigating above-target inflation under new Fed Chair Kevin Warsh. Schmid expresses optimism about the economy's durability while warning that the Fed must continue addressing inflation currently running in the mid-3s.

## Jackson Hole Symposium & The Future of Payments
* **Focus on Payments Innovation:** The Kansas City Fed economic symposium centers on financial innovation in payments, moving toward "atomic settlement" where money transfers and reconciliations occur instantaneously.
* **Operational Goals:** The Federal Reserve ultimately aims to make payments boring while moving $5 trillion to $10 trillion daily through multiple payment pipes.
* **New Systemic Demands:** Instantaneous payments require proven liquidity and a focus on the duration of assets to back immediate settlements securely.

## Labor Force Dynamics & Demographic Shifts
* **Baby Boomer Retirements:** The labor force is undergoing a major structural change with approximately 4 million baby boomers retiring per year.
* **Intellectual Capital Risk:** While retirements create new opportunities, Schmid notes the primary risk is losing institutional knowledge and intellectual muscle.
* **AI Knowledge Transfer:** Banks and Fed economists are actively using artificial intelligence to transfer institutional knowledge from 65-year-old retirees to younger 25-, 35-, and 45-year-old analysts.

## Economic Growth & AI-Driven Commodity Demand
* **Trend State Growth:** Schmid views the economy as growing nicely between 2% and 3.5%, expressing optimism about the durability of the current economic expansion.
* **Data Center and AI Boom:** The build-out of data centers and artificial intelligence is creating heavy commercial credit demand and directly competing with other industries for resources.
* **Commodity and Supply Pressures:** Surging demand is impacting machinery, steel, copper, and even grain futures markets, which complicates the Fed's path back to its 2% inflation target.

## Monetary Policy, Yields, and the Mandate
* **Inflation Concerns:** Schmid emphasizes that the Fed has not finished its job on inflation, noting a recent surge into the mid-3s that must be addressed to fulfill the dual mandate.
* **Price of Money and Yields:** The 10-year Treasury yield and other long-term rates reflect supply and demand dynamics, credit competition between the commercial and public sectors, and a fairly normalized yield curve.
* **Accommodative Financial Conditions:** Schmid assesses current policy rates as relatively accommodative, noting that short-term rates primarily influence immediate decisions like inventory pre-buying, while long-term yields impact decade-long capital projects.

## FOMC Governance & The Warsh Era
* **Open Debate Culture:** Praising both former Chair J. Powell and current Chair Kevin Warsh, Schmid welcomes Warsh's emphasis on transparency and a willingness to accept robust debate rather than top-down mandates.
* **Role of Dissents:** Dissents serve as a mechanism to signal that an FOMC member weighs the risks between full employment and price stability differently than the majority.
* **Task Forces and Communication:** Newly formed task forces are evaluating economic data sets and communication policies, though regional Fed presidents have not yet engaged in direct dialogue with them pending the release of their formal research.

## Notable Quotes
> "We move 5 to 10 trillion dollars a day through the systems, through multiple different pipes... Ultimately as a Federal Reserve [we want] to make payments boring."  
> — Jeffrey Schmid

> "We're signing more retirement letters in the last three months than I have for the last three years, but I worry about the intellectual muscle that we're losing in that."  
> — Jeffrey Schmid

> "We clearly have had a bit of a surge into the mid threes [on inflation]. It has to be addressed, that's our mandate."  
> — Jeffrey Schmid
